name: Karl Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Karl, 58, and I lead developers at a tech company that makes software for hospital medicine cabinets. I have a master’s degree and I’m the person nurses call when a cabinet says a dose is missing but the drawer count is right. I trace the audit log, speak to the ward pharmacist and review a fix before it reaches patients. I use AI now and then to suggest harmless test cases, never with patient records.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household budget like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Leila teaches paid music lessons, and our children are grown. My pay is low for a lead developer in this town, her pupils come and go, and we still have a mortgage. We have about three weeks of expenses saved and few similar developer jobs nearby. Retirement is getting closer, but we have no verified income figure that would pay the bills if we stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the ward AI Plateau still leaves a nurse and pharmacist checking whether the medicine is in the drawer. A perfect log is not a dose in someone’s hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still worry about lesson cancellations and three weeks of savings. My lead post is stable, but we cannot absorb a long quiet spell and a mortgage payment together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking cabinet logs against drawer counts with the ward pharmacist. I’d save 40 after paydays only if mortgage and groceries are covered. In the first year I’d use AI only for invented cabinet cases and retain pharmacist sign-off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about ordinary household bills, despite secure work. The smallest missing payment can use much of our buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which physical pack changed your diagnosis?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A cabinet counted a returned dose as a new issue. I found the duplicate log entry after the nurse showed me the physical pack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you replace the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila and I would keep our older car if it passes inspection. We would not pay for a new one while the savings account is still a few weeks deep.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave medicine checks with pharmacists.
I would compare **cabinet logs** with physical drawer counts.
think: I worry **music pupils** may cancel unexpectedly.
Our **three-week reserve** cannot cover a long quiet spell and mortgage.
do: **Check** cabinet logs against drawer counts with pharmacist approval.
**Use** AI only with invented cabinet tests; keep inspected safe car rather than buy replacement.
feel: **Anxious** about existing bills despite a steady lead post.
S0.quote: A perfect log is not a dose in someone’s hand.
fieldNote: His **lead expertise** connects software logs to physical packs and pharmacist judgment before changes reach patients.
The **three-week buffer** and variable music lessons keep baseline financial anxiety present around mortgage payments.

steps.text: Keep checking medicine cabinet logs against drawer counts with pharmacist sign-off
Save 40 only after mortgage and groceries
Defer replacing old car while it passes inspection

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption can write and check cabinet code before robots carry medicine on wards. I would keep pharmacists responsible for releasing a changed dose rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think management may stop replacing developers and ask my small team to cover more wards. My own pay looks steady this year, but three weeks saved leaves no room for a cut in paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask management for a paid session to learn how to test AI-generated cabinet rules against twenty old, de-identified mismatch cases. I’d try it only with pharmacist review and written approval to keep patient data out of the tool. In the first year, if my hours fall, I’d apply only to real hospital-software vacancies whose written wage with Leila’s usual lessons covers our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my wage if workload targets become hour cuts. I would rather prove a method on old cases than put a guessed rule on a live ward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which mismatch belongs in the test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One old mismatch came from a returned pack that two systems counted differently. The pharmacist’s physical count is what told us which entry was wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would new pupils protect the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila would count paid pupils on the current timetable, not inquiries about lessons. I cannot call a parent’s question income.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to reach cabinet code before ward robots.
I would retain **pharmacist release control** on dose rules.
think: I expect my **lead pay** to hold this year.
I worry **team hours** may be cut under higher ward targets.
do: **Learn** AI rule testing only with approved paid time, twenty de-identified cases and pharmacist review.
**Keep** patient data out of the tool under written approval.
**Apply** if hours fall only to real posts with mortgage-covering written pay.
feel: **Anxious** about possible lost hours and thin savings.
S1.quote: I would rather prove a method on old cases than put a guessed rule on a live ward.
fieldNote: His **AI learning** requires paid approval, de-identified cases, written privacy protection and pharmacist review.
A **job search** begins only after hours fall, with real written pay compared with usual lesson income.

steps.text: Learn AI cabinet tests only with paid approval, twenty de-identified cases and pharmacist review
Apply if hours fall only to real posts with mortgage-covering pay alongside usual lessons

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches cabinet-code thinking work in 2028; hands-on ward robots follow around 2031. A later robot does not keep a software salary alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect even my lead role could be cut if a cheaper system handles the code. Three weeks saved would run out before a long local search, and music pupils could also have less to spend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for written layoff terms and contact the lender before a missed mortgage payment if my post ends. Leila and I would cancel the planned family reunion travel before booking tickets. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply to real paid openings and eligible help, without counting our children’s wages or hoped-for lesson bookings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed and losing sleep about the mortgage. Two years is too short to turn this low lead wage into a retirement cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would grown children fund travel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our children we cannot travel this year. I would not ask them to pay for a reunion we have postponed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who owns a wrong alert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the pharmacist who will own a wrong dose alert if our team is gone. A named person must still answer a nurse.

say: I expect **2028 AGI** to reach cabinet code before 2031 ward robots.
I would demand **named dose-alert responsibility** after software cuts.
think: I expect my **lead post** could be cut.
I know **three weeks saved** cannot bridge scarce local jobs.
do: **Request** written layoff terms and contact lender early if post ends.
**Cancel** family reunion travel before tickets are booked.
**Apply** to real paid openings and eligible help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** and sleepless about losing the main wage.
S2.quote: Two years is too short to turn this low lead wage into a retirement cushion.
fieldNote: He expects **2028 code loss** despite seniority; physical ward robots follow around 2031.
The **thin buffer** drives early lender contact and postponed travel, not assumed family income.

steps.text: Cancel family reunion travel before buying tickets
Apply to real paid openings if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible public help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 still reaches cabinet code in 2031 and ward robots around 2034. Five years gives me a chance to seek better pay from a real hospital-software employer while those jobs still exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect code work to face cuts. A higher salary before 2031 could build savings, but it would not make a new firm safe after full thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d apply to two regional hospital-software firms only if they advertise real paid lead roles. I’d switch only on a signed offer whose net pay after travel is higher, with continuous paid weeks and no loss of health cover; I would put the extra pay in savings. In the first year after 2031, if code work ends, I’d seek actual paid openings and eligible help rather than assume the new employer keeps programmers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about future code jobs, but willing to compare a concrete offer. I cannot afford a week without pay while moving between firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a real offer show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the hiring manager to show the on-call rota and the wage after travel. A lead developer title with unpaid on-call nights would leave us poorer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What income would you count from Leila?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila would keep her usual booked pupils in the household calculation. New lesson inquiries and our children’s wages would stay off it.

say: I expect **2031 AGI** to reach code before 2034 ward robots.
I would seek **higher paid lead work** while real roles exist.
think: I expect **code jobs** could shrink when full thinking AI arrives in 2031.
I cannot assume **another software firm** survives full 2031 AGI merely because it pays more.
do: **Apply** only to two firms’ real paid lead vacancies.
**Switch** only with signed net gain after travel and unpaid on-call nights, continuous paid weeks and health cover.
**Save** extra pay; seek actual openings and eligible help if code ends after 2031.
feel: **Anxious** about code pay, with a chance to improve savings.
S3.quote: A lead developer title with unpaid on-call nights would leave us poorer.
fieldNote: He uses the **five-year warning** to seek higher net wages before full AGI, not a safe refuge.
The **offer gate** protects pay continuity, health cover and savings from a costly commute.

steps.text: Switch only for signed net gain after travel and unpaid nights, continuous pay and health cover
Save extra pay only while the new wage arrives
Seek actual paid openings if code work ends after 2031
Apply for eligible income help if code work ends after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 reaches cabinet code in 2036; hands-on ward robots follow around 2039. A decade gives us time to press for funded transitions and check actual retirement resources.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my pay may hold for a while, but the firm could still squeeze senior hours before 2036. Three weeks saved and no verified retirement figure mean I cannot assume age will make us secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep pharmacist-checked cabinet releases and save 40 on paydays after mortgage and groceries. I’d join the staff association’s transition group and ask each year for funded training and paid ward-support jobs filled. In the first year after 2036, if coding ends, I’d seek real paid work; I would retire only if written income, savings and mortgage figures cover living costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the thin buffer even with ten years. A ten-year warning helps only if my paid developer weeks become savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set a retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request our own retirement statements and compare them with the loan balance. I will not borrow a colleague’s pension story or our children’s wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What cases would you keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the old returned-pack cases as teaching records without patient names. A new developer needs to know what the physical drawer said.

say: I expect **2036 AGI** to reach code before 2039 ward robots.
I would count **funded transitions** by paid ward-support jobs.
think: I worry **senior hours** could be squeezed before 2036.
I know **three weeks saved** cannot fund retirement alone.
do: **Keep** pharmacist-checked releases and save 40 only after essentials.
**Join** association transition group and request yearly funded-training and paid-job counts.
**Seek** real paid work if coding ends after 2036; retire only with verified resources.
feel: **Anxious** about thin savings despite ten years.
S4.quote: A ten-year warning helps only if my paid developer weeks become savings.
fieldNote: He measures **funded transitions** by actual paid ward jobs, not course seats.
Retirement depends on **written income** and mortgage figures, not age or child wages.

steps.text: Keep pharmacist-checked medicine-cabinet releases while paid
Save 40 on paydays only after mortgage and groceries
Join staff association transition group for yearly funded-training and paid-job counts
Seek real paid openings if code ends after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because even a lead can be cut with only weeks of savings. Written terms, a real paid opening, eligible help and a named person for dose alerts would matter. A master’s degree does not pay the mortgage by itself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the nurse to open the drawer before trusting the cabinet log. The medicine is either there or it is not.

headlineQuote: The medicine is either there or it is not.
portrait: Karl is a **58-year-old lead developer** with a master’s degree, lower pay and three weeks saved.
He uses **AI occasionally** on invented medicine-cabinet tests, checking physical packs with pharmacists.
His wife’s **music-lesson income** varies, leaving the mortgage exposed to ordinary cancellations.
He seeks **higher net lead pay** before 2031 only with a signed offer, continuous paid weeks and health cover.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut his lead post before he builds a month of savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Written terms**, real paid work, eligible help and named dose-alert responsibility would matter.
